entry.title: The permission you can't prompt away
entry.summary: Enforcing agent safety in the tool layer, not the system prompt. Drawn from a personal agentic system ("Vantage") I built and run daily. Most agent "guardrails" are sentences. Somewhere in a system prompt there is a line like "Never delete files without asking" or "Do not send email on the user's behalf." The line is polite, it is well-intentioned, and it is not a control. It is a request addressed to a probabilistic text generator, evaluated anew on every turn, competing with everything else in the context window. The day it loses that competition is the day you find out your safety model was a suggestion. I want to argue a narrower and more useful position than "prompts are unreliable," which everyone already knows. The position is: the boundary between what an agent may suggest and what…

entry.title: CrowdSec vs Fail2Ban vs CSF: Choosing Intrusion Prevention for Linux Servers
entry.summary:
CrowdSec vs Fail2Ban vs CSF: Choosing Intrusion Prevention for Linux Servers
A Linux server with a public IP address can start receiving SSH brute-force attempts, automated port scans, and suspicious login requests soon after deployment. A firewall controls which connections are allowed. But what happens when an IP address repeatedly attempts to log in through an exposed SSH service? That's where intrusion prevention tools help. They detect suspicious behavior and can block offending IP addresses before repeated attempts become a bigger problem. Three commonly discussed options are CrowdSec, Fail2Ban, and CSF (ConfigServer Security & Firewall). Here's how they differ and when to consider each one. Fail2Ban monitors logs or the systemd journal for patterns such as repeated failed logins. …

entry.title: Routes, Ingress or Gateway API on OpenShift 4: Which to Choose and How to Migrate
entry.summary: Every OpenShift cluster ships with at least two ways to expose an HTTP service, and since 4.14 there is a third. Route is the native OpenShift object, Ingress is the portable Kubernetes one, and the Gateway API is the upstream replacement for Ingress — implemented on OpenShift by an Istio-based gateway controller managed by the Cluster Ingress Operator. This is not a cosmetic choice. The abstraction you pick determines where TLS is terminated, which timeouts you can tune, whether you can do header manipulation or traffic splitting without a sidecar hack, and which metrics you will have during an incident at 3 a.m. This article compares the three on concrete limits, then walks through migrating a production Route loaded with HAProxy annotations to a Gateway API HTTPRoute with re-encrypt TLS…
